utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning. This is case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. After one week of recess, perhaps I should ask the parties whether there is any specific issue they wanted to bring to the attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the close of last -- two weeks ago, you requested that the Prosecution take all possible steps to ensure that the evidence in the Prosecution case will be completed by the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That process took place last week, and I am reasonably confident that we can do that. I note that there are three days set aside for Plenary session in that period and also a day for court maintenance. I have spoken to the senior legal officer in chambers to see if it is possible for at least the court maintenance date to be shifted, and if we have that additional day, I think that would be extremely useful since it falls on the Friday of the second last week of this additional period. I am hopeful that that could be postponed for six trial days so that it takes place during the break. In any event, I anticipate that as soon as I have word back on that, I can then submit a timetable for the entirety of the remaining period and indicate precise dates for some, if not of all, the experts. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you also mentioned Plenary without attaching any further expectation to that. Well, I noticed that you brought to our attention that it was three days Plenary. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, any specific issue? I see that Ms. Pilipovic is not there. I hope that there is just a practical reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking that question, Mr. President. It is that the planes are not always -- don't always conveniently arrive on time and Ms. Pilipovic will arrive a little later, perhaps at the end of the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, looking at the last schedule, Mr. Ierace, I notice that the next witness the Prosecution will call is Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and Mr. Waespi will take him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber also noticed that there are still two pending witnesses so we have to see where we can fit them in as soon as possible because interruptions, although not always unavoidable, of course should be limited to the extent necessary. Then, Mr. Waespi, are you ready to call Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. AND the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Tucker. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker. Could you please state for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: My name is Pyers William Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could spell your first name.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It is P-y-e-r-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your nationality?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am a UK citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps for practical reasons, if you could slow down while you are talking, because we are talking the same language, and also watch the screen in front of you and only answer my questions when you have seen that the transcript has stopped moving. Can you briefly tell us your military education, also specifically mentioning your specialties in military training.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am a British Army officer and I was trained at Sandhurst, which is the officer training school, in 1976 and 1977. I was then commissioned into the Royal Artillery and I served as a Royal Artillery officer in Germany, Canada, Northern Ireland, Bosnia, and all around the world in other locations. I underwent artillery training at the Royal School of Artillery in 1997 and 1984 and 1986, and conducted concentrations of artillery fire on exercise in Germany and in Canada and in the United Kingdom. I also served in Northern Ireland in an infantry role when my artillery units underwent three months training in order to serve their infantry role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Did you also have experiences as a marksman?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was a skilled marksman and I competed at Bisley, which is the top British marksmanship competition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I served in the former Yugoslavia in 1992 and 1993, in 1995 and 1996 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning to the first period, 1992, 1993, when exactly were you deployed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I arrived in Belgrade around the middle of October 1992 and then deployed into Sarajevo on the 25th, 26th of October, and I then left Sarajevo on the -- at the very end of March. I think it was about the 31st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In what function did you serve in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I was appointed as the military assistant to General Philippe Morillon, and that means it was my responsibility to accompany the General to all the meetings that he went to. And those were meetings with the military and political leaders of all three warring factions and the political and military leaders of Serbia, that is, the country with capital Belgrade, and to Croatia, the country with capital Zagreb. At these meetings, it was my responsibility to take the minutes of those meetings and write the -- draft the reports from those meetings for General Morillon to approve and sign and send on to HQ UNPROFOR in Zagreb, to New York, or to other military commands as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you say that you accompanied General Morillon to see military leaders, what type of military leaders? What level were these people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon dealt with the senior military leaders of all three sides, that is, on the Bosnian Serb side, particularly with General Mladic; on the Bosniak side, particularly with General Halilovic; and on the Bosnian Croat side, it was with Brigadier General Patkovic and sometimes with their immediate junior, immediate subordinate officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, were you involved in drafting written protests to the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I was involved with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I believe that this is a particular leading question because it would imply that the protests would only be addressed to one party, that is the Serb party. Perhaps one could ask a question to find out whether protests were addressed to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first ask in general terms whether any involvement in drafting protests was part of the job of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, was part of your duties and responsibilities to draft written protests to all warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us examples for these written protests.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon was only involved with written protests about the most serious of events, of incidents, and the more general day-to-day ones were handled by the headquarters of Sector Sarajevo for events around Sarajevo and by the headquarters of Bosnia-Herzegovina command, for instance, outside Sarajevo. Examples of instances where I drafted protests were when General Morillon's headquarters in Sarajevo were shelled and mortared on the 24th and 25th of December, 1992. And in that instance, after the research and investigation that I carried out, it was our belief that the first of those attacks was carried out by forces within Sarajevo, and on that instance, the protest was addressed to President Izetbegovic. Another example was when some outgoing fire had come from the Kosevo hospital, mortar fire, and the retaliatory Serb artillery fire came in and some of it was landing very close to General Morillon's headquarters, which was about 400 metres from Kosevo hospital, which is why we became aware of this particular shelling. And in that instance, the protest was addressed to General Mladic in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one brief clarification on what you said. You mentioned that in relation to the Kosevo hospital, there was some outgoing fire that had come from the Kosevo hospital. Was that within the hospital or within the compounds of the hospital area? Do you know more about where the mortars were located that fired?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: On that particular incident, we had reports of fire coming out of the hospital area. I do not have more specific information. But I do have specific information that there was a unit of Bosniak mortar who went into the middle of Kosevo hospital and fired salvos of mortars out of Kosevo hospital, and this was witnessed by a British Army Royal Engineer sergeant who was delivering diesel fuel to the Kosevo hospital, and he saw these people firing because he arrived earlier than expected at the hospital. This was a tactic which was used on a number of occasions in order to invite retaliatory fire by the Serbs, which would then land on the hospital and the area around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Tucker, when you say that the mortar went into the middle of Kosevo hospital, was it placed within the building or was it placed outside the building but on the ground within the hospital area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was obviously not in the building, in a building, because it wouldn't be able to fire. The description of the sergeant was that it was a mortar on the back of a truck, which allowed it to be moved quickly from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. location to location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tucker, when you arrived in Sarajevo, how was the situation? Can you tell us your impressions you had?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo at the end of October 1992, I found a city with a population which was in shock. They were very anxious and very afraid. The city was surrounded by hostile forces who prevented food -- they had cut water supplies, electricity supplies, gas supplies. There was a shortage of food. And later, in the winter, with the cold and the lack of heating, the situation was desperate. Life in Sarajevo was very unpleasant for these people. There were daily random shelling of various parts of the city. There was constant sniper fire and there were intense periods of small arms and artillery fire around the perimeter from time to time as attacks by one side or the other continued. It was a horrible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us about random fire. From which side of the confrontation line and who was responsible for this fire you have described as random?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo, there were two types of incoming fire. There was concentrated fire, in other words, multiple shells landing in a short space of time in a particular area. The second type of fire was single shells landing arbitrarily around the city, to no identifiable purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you talk about no identifiable purpose, can you put that into relation to civilian targets and military targets?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: When I described the concentrated fire, that was usually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone counsel, please. Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please use your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I need to intervene for the transcript. I thought that I heard in the French booth that there were no local targets, but that is not what the witness said, because the witness was saying that he wasn't seeing a particular target or particular objective of these shellings, of single shelling because there were multiple shellings as well. I think he spoke -- he couldn't see the purpose. I don't think we were talking about the targeting. I think that's -- for the purpose of the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...listen to the French channel, but I am certain that proper care will be taken that the French transcript is correct in this respect. Thank you for your assistance. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I had asked you to clarify what you meant by, and I quote, "no identifiable purpose," whether you could put that into relation to military or civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was not to any military purpose. These were shells which were just landing somewhere within Sarajevo. In other words, in the built-up areas, civilian areas. They were not fired at during any attacks or to defend. They simply were fired into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to negotiations you had or you attended with warring parties. Did you have an occasion to meet General Mladic? I think you said initially in the beginning that you in fact accompanied General Morillon to meetings with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct. I met General Mladic on quite a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when was it the first time you met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe it was around the 27th of October, 27th, 28th of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what the subject of this meeting was, what was discussed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That was the first meeting between General Morillon, the newly appointed commander of the UN forces in Bosnia, with General Mladic, the commander of the Bosnian Serb forces, obviously in Bosnia. General Morillon had a number of agenda items. The first was to introduce himself and explain what his objectives were. Secondly, to seek agreement to the deployment of CanBat, that is the 2nd Canadian battalion, into the Banja Luka area. Thirdly, it was to seek a ceasefire throughout Bosnia. Fourthly, it was to seek an improvement to the utilities, that is, gas, water, electricity, into Sarajevo. General Mladic, for his side, made a very strong statement that Republika Srpska was a reality. It existed, had people, customs, forces and authority, and that all communications with them had to be directed to authorities as members of the government of Republika Srpska. Any letters which were not addressed in that manner would be ignored and returned to sender. He also made a strong point, saying that he was only a military commander and that he carried out the instructions of his government and that he did not have the authority, for example, to approve the deployment of CanBat 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did General Mladic, at that meeting, also express his thoughts about the military situation in and of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And I have here the notes that I made at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should not at the very moment, until being invited to do so, consult any notes, Mr. Tucker. So please wait and see what Mr. Waespi will ask you. If it will be necessary to consult them, then please first ask the Court permission to do so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you need to consult them, with leave of the Court, you can do so. If you are able to do that without the notes, that would be preferable or fine as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to just use this opportunity: In English transcript, 10.18, it should be mentioned CanBat 2, and that doesn't appear in the transcript

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is my recollection that in earlier instances, the witness was referring to CanBat 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could have a minute, Mr. President, to consult with Mr. Ierace, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can do without the notes, that would be preferable, whether you recall the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think if -- it is all very well to say that if we can do without the notes, that is fine, but not with the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...in order to make clear that you are not consulting your notes, perhaps you better close them. That is what Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to see done. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Tucker, have you shown these notes to the Prosecution? Are these notes you gave copies to the Prosecution previously?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, I was not clear enough. Have you given these notes to members of the Office of the Prosecutor previously?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: About a year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of the persons you have given these notes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Caroline Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So perhaps, having closed your notes, you can answer my question about the comments General Mladic made about the military situation in Sarajevo, how he saw his policy in relation to Sarajevo, then please answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to be clear on these matters, considering that this witness practically already consulted his notes, perhaps we could ask him if he has already seen his answer in the notes. Perhaps he has already consulted his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether he consulted his notes. I saw him opening a binder. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tucker, can you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Mladic made a number of points regarding Sarajevo. He said that there were two solutions to Sarajevo. The first was that Sarajevo was split in two and that the Bosniaks stayed in the old city and that UNPROFOR provided a separation force to keep the two sides apart. The second solution was for the Bosniaks to surrender all their arms and weapons to UNPROFOR and for UNPROFOR to guarantee that no fire, no shooting, would occur against Serbs. And General Mladic then laughed and said, "There is, of course, a third solution and that is for them to surrender, but then I don't think that is what they will do."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did General Mladic use the example of another city to explain what he meant?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Mladic, for the splitting of Sarajevo, used the example of Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting, was there any military operation which followed and which reminded you of this meeting you had?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: About two or three days later, there came a major attack by the Bosnian Serb forces surrounding Sarajevo in which they tried for the last time to capture Sarajevo or, more specifically, to cut it in half. They attacked from the north and the south just to the west of the old city and this was a very fierce and sustained attack, using infantry and heavy weapons. But the sustained defence by the Bosniaks prevented them from making much progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did this military operation last for?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It lasted for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall the date the operation started or how long it was after the meeting you had with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was on the 31st of October and I can't recall, without referring to my notes that I made at the time, whether it was the 1st of November or the 30th October as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Were you involved in negotiations about the departure of Serb and Croatian citizens from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I was not personally involved in these negotiations but became aware of them, firstly, because of reports from headquarter Sector Sarajevo, which had been involved with these negotiations before General Morillon and I arrived in Sarajevo. And secondly, because Dr. Ganic, a member of the Bosniak Presidency, told General Morillon about these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you be a little bit more specific about the contents of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: These negotiations were about the evacuation of several thousand Croats from Sarajevo to Split and several thousand Serbs to Belgrade, using buses provided by Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At one time, was there an intervention from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: We were told by headquarters Sector Sarajevo around the 4th, 5th of November, 1992, that Colonel Zarkovic, a Bosnian Serb colonel, had sent a message saying that if the Serb convoy was not allowed to leave the city by 1300 hours that day, that he would shell the city. General Morillon had a meeting with Dr. Ganic that morning and Dr. Ganic told General Morillon the same thing, in other words, that the Presidency had received a message from Colonel Zarkovic saying what I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Dr. Ganic was and then who Colonel Zarkovic was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Dr. Ganic was the vice-president of the Presidency in Sarajevo. And Colonel Zarkovic was a senior commander of Bosnian Serb forces surrounding Sarajevo who attended many of the negotiations which General Morillon had with commanders on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now you told us that, and I quote you: "He," meaning Colonel Zarkovic, "would shell the city." By "shelling the city," what is meant?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: My understanding was that this was a threat and the execution of the threat implied the firing of artillery shells at random into Sarajevo, in other words, at the civilian population in Sarajevo. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, did you have a chance to meet General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I met General Galic on a number of occasions. The first particular occasion was on the 14th of November, 1992, when General Morillon wanted to meet General Mladic, but General Mladic was heavily involved with an emergency in the Trevinje area in south-east where Croatian forces were attacking into Bosnia. So General Mladic requested General Morillon meet General Galic instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show a document to the witness, and since it is a protected document, we should, with your leave, turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to question the witness about it and if it will be shown, then it is preferable to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Redacted – Closed Session – Pages 9910-9918

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it confirmed on my screen that we are now in open session again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, did you have occasions to attend meetings which included Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon and I met with Lord Owen at the beginning of December, together with Vance in Split. The second time was for about four or five days, from around the 17th or 18th of December at 1992, when Lord Owen stayed at the residency with General Morillon in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what was said between General Mladic -- between General Morillon, Lord Owen, and the parties they talked to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: There was much which was said between particularly Lord Owen and General Mladic, but the most memorable event was when Lord Owen chastised General Mladic and told him that the shelling of Sarajevo was an absolute disgrace and had to stop. General Mladic went red in the face, stood up and shouted and banged the table. And Lord Owen talked to Mladic in a schoolmasterly fashion, talking to a little boy. It was only when Professor Koljevic intervened and changed the subject that tempers calmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall similar exchanges about this subject between General Morillon and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon on many occasions said to General Mladic and to Karadzic that history would judge the Serbs and their actions by the way that he used his artillery and that he had to understand this and that it was in his own interests to stop his artillery from firing into cities and towns and at civilians. This was something which General Morillon said on many occasions and something to which General Mladic usually responded by saying something along the lines of his heavy weapons being equivalent to the Bosniak infantry. His forces had few infantry but many heavy weapons, whereas the Bosniaks had a lot of infantry but few heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarifying three names which you mentioned, what were the positions of Lord Owen, Mr. Vance and Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Lord Owen and Mr. Vance were members of a party seeking to assist the warring factions in the former Yugoslavia find an agreement under which they could live together in peace. Professor Koljevic was a member of the Serb Presidency and an advisor to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Was there an attempt by the Bosnian Muslim army to break out of Sarajevo, which you observed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosniaks carried out a major offensive at the beginning of December 1992 to try and break the siege of Sarajevo. They carried out a pincer attack from Otes and Stup from Ilidza and from Butmir from the other side. Simultaneously, they carried out a number of other attacks from inside Sarajevo in order to confuse the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb forces and to prevent them from being able to focus their defence in the area where their main effort was, which was Ilidza. The fighting lasted a couple of weeks and was very intense with vicious house-to-house fighting and the use of many heavy weapons. The attack caught the Bosnian Serb army by surprise and the Bosniaks initially made some progress. Once the Bosnian Serbs was able to bring reinforcements and professional infantry and tanks and heavy weapons to the area, the Bosnian Serbs carried out a sustained series of attacks and captured Otes and part of Stup, pushing the Bosniaks back from where they had originally started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did they do that, the Bosnian Serb army? What were you able to observe from your sources?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb army used classical housefighting tactics with small groups of well-trained infantry with the support of heavy fire-power provided by tanks, artillery, and mortars, and fought their way, house by house, through Otes and halfway through Stup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we are close to 10.30. If you can find a suitable moment to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that will be one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Pilipovic. I am glad to see that you did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been informed already about the practical problems that kept you out of this courtroom. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, just before we broke for the recess, you talked about the events at Otes the beginning of December and you described that the Bosnian Serbs used infantry but also other weapons such as artillery. Can you describe the role of artillery? Did they support the infantry or also had they a role on their own?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The artillery was used in two ways. Firstly, it was used in the immediate support of the attacks by the Bosnian Serb infantry, but the artillery was also used firing all over the city at targets which had nothing to do with the actual attack which had been carried out by the Bosniak forces. The impression that we gained was that the purpose of this shelling was in order to intimidate, firstly, the population of Sarajevo in general and to break their will to resist; and secondly, in order to intimidate the Presidency of Alija Izetbegovic and break their will to resist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This observation, did you make it only at the occasion of these events around Otes in early December 1992 or also at other times?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, this was a tactic which was used by the Bosnian Serb forces throughout the time that I was in Sarajevo, and it was as follows: A Bosniak infantry attack would commence in a particular area. The attack, if it was successful, would gain some ground because the Bosnian Serb perimeter was not held by nearly as many soldiers as the Bosniaks had. The Bosnian Serb army would use artillery tanks, armoured vehicles, heavy machine-guns, anti-aircraft guns used in the ground fire drill in order to stabilise the situation and then push back the Bosniaks. They would then carry out what we would describe as punitive shelling of the area of the city out of which the infantry attack had been mounted, and this was something we observed time and time again. And the sense that we had about this was that it was, again, to punish the citizens in the area from which the attack had come and to demonstrate how useless it was to resist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On Christmas Eve 1992, were you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: On Christmas Eve, I was standing outside the Residency together with a couple of other staff officers from General Morillon's headquarters and suddenly, at midnight, every single artillery gun, mortar, tank, machine-gun, around Sarajevo started firing in a huge barrage into Sarajevo for about 20 minutes. For example -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have to intervene for a question of interpretation. I don't think that what was the -- that there was no barrage fire but it was barrage type of shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that this will be properly reflected now in the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This fire was coordinated and all started at one moment, and a huge amount of ammunition was expended. It looked like a fireworks demonstration, there was that much ammunition fired, except that this was a lethal fireworks demonstration. I am an artillery officer and I know how much coordination it takes in order to arrange for so many weapons in so many different locations to be manned at midnight on Christmas Eve, to have the artillery ammunition in place, to have the targets coordinated in order to achieve what was carried out that evening. For example, there was a 40-millimetre Bofors anti-aircraft gun positioned above the Residency, and the gunner of this gun fired, boom-boom, boom-boom-boom, boom-boom. Boom-boom, boom-boom-boom, boom-boom. Each time, a 40-millimetre shell being fired into the city for 20 minutes in that rhythm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your opinion or your observations, did these weapon systems engage any military targets or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: There were very few military targets in Sarajevo which could be engaged by heavy weapons. These weapons fired at civilian targets at random across the length and breath of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, which army did these weapons systems belong to which were active on Christmas Eve, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: These weapons were firing from the mountains and high ground around Sarajevo, and the impacts of the weapons were inside Sarajevo and, therefore, could only have been weapons of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And also in terms of clarifications, you already touched upon this issue of coordination, but can you pronounce on the role of the commanders to initiate or supervise or coordinate such an action, perhaps discussing commanders at the higher level?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The usage of such large amounts of ammunition had to have been approved at a fairly high level. To arrange for the gun crews to have all the transport necessary, to arrange for them to be on the gun positions at that unusual time in order to be able to fire this -- I will not use the word "barrage" -- this concentration of fire, can only have been carried out by the order of, and with the approval of, the senior most commanders of the Bosnian Serb army surrounding Sarajevo. The communications required in order to coordinate this can only have passed through the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb forces surrounding Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The actual date of this event, you said Christmas Eve. What date is that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is using the Christian calendar. That is the 24th of December, and I am not familiar -- I can't recall the terminology, but it is not the Greek Orthodox calendar that I am using.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to observe a similar event later?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. A similar event happened on the Christmas Eve according to the Greek Orthodox calendar, which was on the 7th of January of 1993, which was the 24th of December according to the Greek Orthodox calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was it exactly the same 20-minute operation or was it any different in time or manner than what you have described earlier?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was a very similar event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown the next exhibit, which is 530, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: This document was drafted by headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Kiseljak for the mixed military working group, which was a meeting which occurred regularly at headquarters -- at -- usually at the airport between two or three of the warring factions, with the purpose of trying to bring about a ceasefire around Sarajevo, freedom of movement for civilians and the repair of utilities and the resumption of normal living. This agreement was one of the agreements reached in the mixed military working group and it agreed corridors for the freedom of movement of civilians around Sarajevo and into and out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. The date this agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, considering the period of the recess that we had, it seems that we did not receive the Serbian translations of this document. It may have happened that we received them in the pigeon hole very recently, but we were not able to check this. So perhaps if the Prosecution could give us these translations so that at least General Galic could try and follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This version has been disclosed on the 3rd of June, which would mean a bit more than 10 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct, Mr. President, on the 3rd of June, before potential exhibits were disclosed in B/C/S. But I am sure we can find a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I do have a copy which could be handed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you could assist us with the date of this agreement and also the parties who eventually signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: This agreement was signed on the 13th of December, 1992, and the parties who signed it were Colonel Siber on behalf of the Bosniak Presidency, by General Gvero on behalf of the Bosnian Serb forces, and by Dario Kordic on behalf of the HVO, the Bosnian Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the position of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Gvero played a subordinate role to General Mladic and deputised for General Mladic on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could turn to the second page on that document, it is the number, usual eight-digit number 00095017, and I see that the first two lines talks about the Security Council Resolution 787. How much of a role played these Security Council resolutions in your work?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The Security Council resolutions were effectively known as that of UNPROFORs' senior orders and instructions and mission statements. And we attempted to carry out the United Nations forces' part of the responsibility to support the implementation of the Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that a frequent topic among the parties in discussions or negotiations, the existence of Security Council resolutions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Security Council resolutions were always mentioned, particularly when a new Security Council resolution had just been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying the parties were aware of the existence of the Security Council resolutions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Absolutely. For example, General Mladic made a big play of Security Council resolutions requiring forces outside of Bosnia to be either removed from Bosnia and to play no part in Bosnia in his arguments that the Croatian forces in Bosnia, that is forces of the Republic of Croatia, in the south-east of Bosnia, near Trebinje and in the north of Bosnia by the river Sava, had to be removed from Bosnia, and why was the international community and the Security Council not condemning Croatia for failing to implement those Security Council resolutions

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Waespi, may I ask you for one clarification. The documents P350 consist of five pages. We just heard that this was an agreement between the parties. I find one page with the words "the mixed military working group," at least where it starts with, and another page that is "Agreement: Freedom of movement linked with the safety of the airport." I see both of these pages -- one's signed by what seems to me Dario Kordic. I see both pages signed by Gvero. And then if it comes to Siber Stjepan, I just see one of these pages that is "Agreement of freedom of movement for civilians linked with the safety of the airport." You didn't ask any questions about that. Is that still to come or -- it is a bit of a puzzle to us, at least to me, but perhaps to the other members of the Chamber, why we find two signed pages by two of the parties but only one signed page by the third party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Tucker, if you could assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If am too early but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could assist His Honour in clarifying these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see, the first page seems to be signed by Siber Stjepan, that is the agreement. Then the second page of the document, which is mixed military working group, signed by Gvero, and then the next page is again the agreement, which seems to be the same document as the one signed by Siber Stjepan, also signed by Gvero. And then we have these two documents signed by Kordic. Why is there only one page signed by Siber Stjepan or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. He signed both and as did the others, and I have no idea why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why we only have five pages instead of six. So it is still a puzzle for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I may move to another subject, Mr. Tucker, that is the crossing of the people of the airport. Do you have any knowledge about people crossing the airport?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The airport was handed over by the Bosnian Serbs to the United Nations during the summer under something that was known as "the Airport Agreement," which stipulated that the airport was only to be used by the United Nations and United Nations' personnel for United Nations activities. Now, the airport was also like the cork in the bottle of the siege around Sarajevo. In other words, if you were a Bosniak and you could get to the airport settlements and you then were able to cross the airport to Butmir, you would not pass through Serb military lines. Now, in the winter, and in particular in January and February when it was coldest, there was no heating, food was short, the shelling was continuing, the snipering was continuing and morale amongst the civilians in Sarajevo was very low, many Bosniaks tried to go to the airport settlement, wait until it was dark, and then tried to run across the airport to Butmir. Now, the French Battalion stationed at the airport had the very unpleasant responsibility of protecting the airport and preventing unauthorised use of the airport, which included preventing the civilians from running across it. About 200 French soldiers, every night, spent all night driving up and down the airport in their vehicles, trying to catch these civilians and taking them back to where they came from, which almost in all cases was back to the airport settlements. Now the French Battalion reported every day how many people they had caught and returned back to the airport settlements, and these figures were a very powerful indicator, barometer, of the state of morale of the city. Another aspect of these civilians trying to run across the airport was that the Bosnian Serbs had set up snipers with nightsights and machine-guns with nightsights and they fired at the civilians trying to run across the airport. And in January and February, every night, between 5 and 20 or 30 civilians were killed or injured by these snipers. And the Serb snipers were not particularly careful about who they fired at and they also killed and injured a number of the French soldiers who were trying to round up the escaping civilians to return them.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. line 1 until up to line 8, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Please continue without naming particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I apologise. The second source of information was the daily situation report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but this way of intervening with the witness doesn't seem very honest because if the witness has people to name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...mentioning names as such, there is nothing wrong with that. But if you guide the witness in such a way that if you expect that a name would be mentioned which might be the name of a protected witness, that you then refer the witness not to mention at that specific moment, the name. So if questions are more generally put to the witness, we cannot ask him not to mention any names, but if it comes to a specific source, then you could perhaps guide the witness, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The second source was the daily situation reports completed by headquarters Sector Sarajevo, which reported what had happened at the airport and gave the statistics of how many Bosniaks had been caught and returned because this was a subject of great concern to General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. I have a couple of more issues before we conclude. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit number 653.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a press clipping dated 9th January, 1993, and I would like you, Mr. Tucker, to read out on the last page of this three-page document, the first three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: On page M0009244?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: At the top of the page, I read: "Mr. Turajlic was pronounced dead on arrival. All seven bullets had hit his body, three of them in the chest, according to a UN official. General Morillon said he was told that Bosnian Serb authorities arrested the soldier who killed Mr. Turajlic. General Morillon demanded the disciplining of General Stanislav Galic, who commands the Bosnian Serb Lukavica Corps. General Morillon said the size and fire-power of the force at the roadblock indicated General Galic must have sent it."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Can you in all briefness explain to us what this incident about Mr. Turajlic was about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: This incident was started by the arrival in Sarajevo airport of a Turkish Air Force C-130 Hercules which carried on board five tonnes of humanitarian aid, and we understand some senior Turkish government officials and some Turkish paratroops. For some reason, the UNHCR air bridge had accepted the offer of this aircraft from the Turkish government in order to deliver humanitarian aid. This was something which had not happened before and the UNHCR had not previously accepted the use of any Turkish aircraft because of the danger of accusations of partiality. Nonetheless, this aircraft arrived. Unbeknown to the United Nations, Mr. Turajlic had climbed on board the shuttle armoured personnel carrier, which carried cleaners from inside the city to Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can stop you just briefly. Who was Mr. Turajlic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Mr. Turajlic was the deputy prime minister, I believe, of the Bosniak Presidency in Sarajevo. He was a senior government official. Mr. Turajlic had boarded this bus, an armoured personnel carrier, with cleaners in the morning who were taken to Sarajevo airport and then brought back in the evening. He had not been notified to the United Nations as a senior government official because normally, when they do that, we provide an escort to ensure their safe movements to or from the airport. What happened at the airport was that the Turkish paratroops fanned out and surrounded the Turkish Air Force aircraft, and Mr. Turajlic had a meeting with the Turkish government delegation. I say again, all this was without the knowledge of the United Nations. Mr Turajlic then climbed back aboard the shuttle bus with the cleaners in order to go back into Sarajevo, but by this time, the Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo, having seen a Turkish aircraft land, having seen Turkish paratroopers dismount from the aircraft, were clearly very suspicious and they dispatched a strong force to block the road between Sarajevo airport and the city. And they stopped every single UN vehicle coming from the airport and demanded to inspect the inside of the vehicle because they believed that weapons, ammunition, personnel, may have been being smuggled into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there for one moment. You don't need to go into too much detail about this incident. If the Defence wants to do that, they are welcome. I also would like you not to again mention any specific names.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The force which carried out the block and which then led subsequently to the tragic killing of Mr. Turajlic inside the back of the UN armoured vehicle, that force was professional Bosnian Serb army soldiers and tanks and was larger than a company, and had to have been commanded at least by a battalion commander, and could not have been deployed, in General Morillon's opinion, without the explicit approval of General Galic. And General Morillon, when he met with General Mladic after the incident, demanded that, firstly, General Galic be disciplined for this event, and secondly, that the Bosnian Serb soldier who had fired the shots which killed Mr. Turajlic also be disciplined and subject to the due processes of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you heard anything back from General Mladic on the fulfillment of the request General Morillon made?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon asked General Mladic on a number of occasions of what had happened and what he had done. And regarding General Galic, General Mladic gave no answer. And regarding the soldier who had killed Turajlic, he said that he had taken that soldier into custody and that he was a 19 year-old soldier, both of whose parents had been killed by the other side - in other words, the Bosniaks - and that he was subject to the discipline of the Bosnian Serb army, but he never informed us what the outcome of that discipline was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. My last point refers to something you said earlier about the incident at Kosevo hospital where Bosnian Muslim troops fired from that compound. Did you have any information that Bosnian Muslim forces shelled their own people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have had many conversations with many people about that. I have not seen any hard evidence or reports to say that. I, however, have seen what I would consider to be strong circumstantial evidence that that happened on a number of occasions and that there were elements within the Bosniak Presidency and the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina who would certainly mentally and psychologically be able to do that. An example was the calling of a press conference at the Kosevo hospital, but this mobile mortar detachment fired out from Kosevo hospital half an hour previously, resulting in a Serb counterbombardment, despite knowing that they were shelling a hospital, as the journalists were arriving for the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Tucker, you said you have seen -- I quote you, "seen what I would consider to be strong circumstantial evidence." But you said earlier that you have seen no reports. What kind of strong circumstantial evidence was that? Did you ever attend a scene when that happened?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, I did not consider any scenes, however, I know that, for example, in the case I have just described, that there was a mobile mortar detachment which frequently fired out of Kosevo hospital, as witnessed by the sergeant who I referred to earlier. And I know that the hospital was usually shelled in response and that usually, whenever the Bosniaks fired out of the city, the Serbs always tried to fire a counterbombardment in order to punish and deter that from happening. Another example which I witnessed myself was when the Bosniaks positioned mortars immediately next to General Morillon's headquarters in Sarajevo and then carried out 20 minutes of rapid fire and then quickly moved away. In fact, that happened for the first time on the very first night that we were in Sarajevo and happened a number of times thereafter. And on each occasion, I immediately made contact with Dr. Ganic to protest and tell him to get his army under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving the opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, may I ask on one clarification. You have been asked about the BiH military firing at their own people. All the examples you have given were BiH firing soliciting for counterfire. Is that what you said by "firing at your own people"? You have told us this morning already about firing from the Kosevo hospital and then it was under the heading of using hospital grounds to fire from. And now you come with similar examples in response to a question of firing at your own people. Does that mean that there was no direct firing, but it was just a soliciting counterfiring to your own people, or was there any direct fire from the BiH to their own people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any hard evidence of them deliberately firing at their own people. What I have just described is where they carried out an action soliciting, as you say, of counterfire. I have heard of two particular incidents when they actually allegedly fired at their own people. One was at a funeral at -- at the big funeral, the big cemetery north of Kosevo hospital, but that was before I arrived in Sarajevo. And people from headquarters Sector Sarajevo, and I can name them if you need, told me that they had carried out investigations, they had actually had some people on the ground, and that they believed that that fire had come from Bosniak forces. And there was a second incident which was, I believe, called the first marketplace shelling, when a large number of civilians were killed in the marketplace by a shell which came into the marketplace. And, again, I have spoken with a number of people about that, but I have no hard evidence to support that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And no personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification. Ms. Pilipovic, is it you or will it be Mr. Piletta-Zanin who will cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be my colleague, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I start by asking the assistance of a technician because my computer which is in front of me, as opposed to the other one, is not functioning and then perhaps I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin to have his computers functioning. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to ask you some questions immediately in relation -- in relation to what you have just spoken of. You just said, sir, that you could name people, those people who conducted investigations on one hand, those involving firing on a funeral, and on the other hand, what you called the incident, "the first marketplace incident."

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please give me the names of the people who investigated, on one hand, the incident at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That was Major Jackson, a Canadian Army officer who was the operations officer at HQ Sector Sarajevo. And secondly, Colonel Bezkrocenko, who was the Chief of Staff of headquarters Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you spell the name of Colonel Bezkrocenko, please, so that we can be absolutely certain about his name?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It is a Ukrainian name. By memory, it's B-e-z-r-o-u-c-h-e-n-k-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, it is possible that I may interrupt you or ask you to stop. That is not that I would want to be rude, that is just trying to gain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time. Thank you. Now, could you please tell us the name, if you know, of the people who investigated the second incident?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Major Itani, who is a Canadian artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: He is the only one who I believe was involved. There were others. There were some senior noncommissioned officers from the British Army, but I don't recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, could you tell us the dates of these two events, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The cemetery incident was before I arrived. I would guess it was about August or September, maybe even earlier. The second event, the marketplace event, was afterwards but I cannot, without referring to my notes, find out when that was, remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Since you have your notes, I am almost certain that the Prosecution will agree with me, I think the moment has come to use them, with the agreement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may consult your notes in respect of the dates -- of the date of the second event you were questioned about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that I cannot recall the date, and to find it would mean me having to read through my notes. These are handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I understand the problem, but perhaps -- could you perhaps in the next break try and find the date - that would pose no problem - and after you have done it, maybe you can let us know. Now, could you tell us briefly what happened in the marketplace? First of all, where this happened and then what was the scale of the victims in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: My understanding of what happened is that a mortar bomb or an artillery shell came down near vertically to land in the marketplace and to cause many casualties to the closely packed civilians who were in the marketplace. And, again, I can't remember the exact details but there were 40 dead. It was some horrific number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, could I stop you there, please. You said that this shell almost fell almost vertically. But could you perhaps tell us where was the market in question located?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The marketplace was in the old town in Sarajevo, which had high buildings on all sides around it. And, therefore, for a shell to come into the marketplace, it would have to have come nearly vertical or pretty close to vertical. If that shell had been fired from a long way away, it would have come in at a much flatter trajectory. And again, as an artillery officer, that is an obvious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am listening to your answer at the same time as the French booth. For the French booth, it is an artillery officer, not a military officer, and I believe this is where it is important to underline the difference. That is exactly what you said, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you spoke of buildings that were relatively high. Now, as far as you know, were these buildings 7, 8-storey buildings? 10-storey buildings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but it was at least four storey, maybe even higher. Maybe some higher than four storeys on some sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, therefore, and according to your experience, technical experience, that is, you as an artillery officer, if we have a four-storey building as you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours. I am not sure whether that is a very -- that it assists you what my learned colleague is doing now. We don't know yet when it happened. We don't know whether the witness was in fact there in that time. Perhaps before he draws on any type of experience or expertise or whatever, I think this should first be clarified, the position of the witness vis-a-vis this incident, and perhaps it could be postponed until the witness knows where he was at the time this incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness has by himself said, following the questions that were asked by the Prosecution, not by your Chamber, mentioned existence of a marketplace. And I asked him what was the location. He will tell us the location later. And as far as the time frame is concerned, the date that it happened, I would say that this is less important than we may think, since what we are also trying to establish here is the possibility, the probability, of people from Sarajevo firing at themselves. Now, if this witness knows something, then he must say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness has testified that he has no personal knowledge of anything, so then at least I think we should find out about what he is talking about. He is talking about the first market. Well, we have heard evidence on markets as well. So I think that Mr. Waespi is right when he says that whatever confusion should be avoided, especially since the witness has no personal knowledge of it, that we identify exactly what we are talking about. So if you would please try to guide the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that you don't have personal knowledge of this. Now, was this an incident that had taken place before you arrived in Sarajevo or did it take place after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It took place after I arrived, the marketplace one. The cemetery one occurred before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And you left -- could you please remind us of the date?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was about the 31st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So the incident, did it happen in the same year, the year that you left or did it happen later?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It may have happened while I was still there, but it could well have happened after I left. And I came back to that when I was working in the United Kingdom Crisis Management Headquarters when we were reviewing information. That was when I was working as a United Nations -- as a United Kingdom officer, not as a United Nations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is it true that you spoke of the first marketplace incident?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So would you then speak also of the second, third, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have heard from the media about a second marketplace incident. However, my knowledge of that is only from what I have read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, this second marketplace incident, would it correspond to the name of Markale? If that means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will see the question of the dates later on, but we can see now that we are probably in the right time frame since the witness said it may have happened while he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spoke of a building, a four-storey building as being a high building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said that as an artillery officer that it was practically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I would like to hear first whether the witness was present, what his relation was to this incident. He is not here as an expert, despite the fact that he had some artillery expertise. But this witness is here to talk about facts, perhaps about information he had heard from somebody else, but not about him going or placing him into an incident we don't know where he was at that time and to have him make any assessments of the highness of building and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Waespi, of course you can ask specific questions and if Mr. Piletta-Zanin wants to spend the time as he wants to and leaving aspects of what you consider to be major importance rather vague, then, of course it might be of importance in the evaluation of that evidence, but he is still entitled to ask questions. On the other hand, I do agree that the more we stick to facts, the more useful it will be to hear the evidence for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, sir, to come back to the facts, you explained to us earlier about the obstacle that was the high building, as indicating by your hand movement. And my impression was that you wanted to tell us something else. In other words, would it have been technically possible that someone from top of a roof would launch by hand such a shell in order to have it explode further down, that would explode at the foot of the building? Would it be technically feasible?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I would believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You believe so, and in a hypothesis of the first marketplace incident, if you know that, do you know what were the conclusions of the investigation commission?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: They were inconclusive. "Inconclusive" was the word I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say that they were inconclusive, what you are saying is politically inconclusive?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No. I mean from the evidence gathered by the technical investigation officer, in other words, Major Itani, he was unable to conclude specifically where that explosive device had been fired from. In other words, he was unable to determine whether it had been fired from Serb lines or from within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, just a -- simply a technical point - we will go to other matters later - now the vertical feature of the angle of the launch, that is an element that in general would allow one to conclude that this was something that was fired from the inside?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The conclusion that I drew personally is that it had to be fired from fairly close by. Now, whether that "close by" was inside or outside the perimeter Sarajevo, that is something I am not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, when you say "close by" could you perhaps, in terms of distance, tell the Chamber on what you can visualise in saying this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That would depend on the size of the shell that was fired. In other words, if it was a small mortar, the distance would be shorter, but if it was a big mortar, that distance would be small in comparison with the maximum range of a big mortar. It is unlikely that it could have been an artillery shell, in my opinion, because artillery fires much flatter, whereas mortars fire much higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, practically, can we speak of several hundreds of metres, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it would be more than several hundreds of metres. It would be depending on the calibre and I can't recall what Major Itani said. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, I am going to ask you a series of questions and I would like you to answer just by "yes" or "no" every time in order to gain time. Do you know in Sarajevo the names or rather the locations, names of places that I am going to give you? I am going to start with Gras, G-r-a-s.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what is Gras and where was this located?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I would need to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe it is a hill or something to do with a hill to the north, north-west of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us what is Magros?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am not similar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Same question for Pavle Goranin.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It is not a name that I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Same question for Kulin Ban.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, not a name I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Same question for Petar Dakic.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, not a name that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Same question for Kobra?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Not a name that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Kobra Fatih?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Not a name that I particularly connect to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sultan Fatih?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Ljiljana?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: MUP, M-u-p?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The Hero Square?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Electrical supply company, Elektropriveda?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The electrical supply company is outside of Sarajevo on the way to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
