utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now, were you informed or are you informed of a school in Dobrinja that had -- that was used as a base for BH snipers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you please tell us the locations, that is, the addresses of all of the brigades that covered of what I sometimes call "the Greater Sarajevo," that is all the municipalities of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: On which side? By the Bosniak side or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am talking about the city of Sarajevo. The city itself and, therefore -- there were two sides, obviously. There was one Croatian brigade and the others were BH brigades. Could you tell us the locations of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the locations, and I can tell you now what I do know is that when I was serving in Sarajevo, that I had maps which showed their locations. And with those maps, I would be able to tell you where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you know where were the command posts of each of the battalions of each of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, that is not a level of detail that General Morillon dealt with and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you personally know where the companies, the command and control posts, not of the level of battalions, [In English] the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We visited General Halilovic's headquarters. He had two particular locations that we visited frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But I was talking about the command post on the level of companies.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, I would now like to come back to the ceasefires. I have to say that we have had testimonies saying that, at the same time when the Serb side wanted to agree to a ceasefire for Sarajevo, that the Bosnian side, the BH side, did not wish it. Were you informed of this and of such situations? Did they occur while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that sort of situation happened frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, I have to tell you that we have also had testimonies that tended to say also in a similar vein to what you have said already, is that when practically ceasefires started operating, the BH army or elements of the BH army would then start firing provocation shots in order to provoke return fire and, therefore, that would cancel out the ceasefire and the agreements. Were you informed of this? Did you know of this during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Yes, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that sort of thing happening fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since we are talking about BH shots, sir, did you know about the existence of special units? So these were sniper units on the side of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you know if these units were established by elements from the police and those elements were at the time established or known as "special units"? They were created during the Olympic Games in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I do not know whether they were police, civilians with special marksmanship skills, or soldiers. The difficulty was that, in Sarajevo, almost any male who had carried out military service could be described as a soldier, and the clothes that they wore, in other words, the uniform, was a very poor indicator of whether someone was a soldier or a civilian or a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you perhaps elaborate on this point in terms of what you said? In terms of what you said in effect that the clothes that were worn would not allow for an immediate identification to tell apart a civilian from a soldier from a policeman, that is, you couldn't tell apart the police from a soldier and a civilian? You couldn't tell them apart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: There were certainly situations when that happened. There were other situations when you were on the front line and when people were fully equipped with military uniforms. There were other situations when you were dealing with police and they were wearing obviously police uniforms. But when you are dealing with refugees or dealing with fluid situations, when you were dealing with people fleeing for their lives wearing whatever clothes they had, you need to take into account that most civilians in Bosnia, all had a considerable amount of ex-military clothing. And the military clothing was of higher quality and warmer, particularly in the winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier spoke of a "fluid situation." Could you tell us what you meant by that? What is a "fluid situation"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: By "fluid situation," I mean where events are happening really quickly and it is difficult to establish what exactly is happening. For example, the fall of Jajce in the end of October, beginning of November 1992, and, for example, the situation surrounding Srebrenica in February and March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, since we have to focus on Sarajevo, by "fluid situations," what you mean is, if I understand correctly, these situations that we can really describe as being emergency situations? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, emergency combat situations, heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, were there situations or emergency situations, emergency combat situations - and I believe that your answer would be affirmative - in the areas that were near or neighbouring or in civilian areas? Would you like me to rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, were these emergency situations, emergency combat situations, in areas that were neighbouring to -- neighbouring areas that were inhabited by civilians?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The fighting always occurred somewhere. When the fighting occurred in built-up areas, then yes, it is possible that there were civilians in that area. I cannot make a generalisation as to whether or not civilians stayed when heavy fighting occurred or not. That is absolutely situation-by-situation dependent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. Should we now have the break at half?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should we have a break now at half past?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...already a couple Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of minutes late.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This moment is perfect. Mr. President, could we just ask the witness to check the date

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...consult your notes and find the date of the second incident called "the first market."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let us now go back to what you were talking about a while ago. You told us that you could find the date of this second, which was the first incident, according to what the President told us. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The date is after I left Bosnia and I don't have it -- the reason I don't have it in my notes and I couldn't find it is because it was after I left. And the only time it could have been was while I was in Srebrenica. But I now recollect where I found a detail about that and it was in 1995, when I was in the headquarters of the 1st UK Armoured Division in Germany and I met the senior noncommissioned officer who had carried out the investigation, and he knew that I had been in Bosnia and he showed me the report which had been completed. And that is from where I recalled a number of items which I described to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But you haven't found the date of the event?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: No, because I don't have it written in the notes because it was after I left Bosnia in the 31st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, have you any other notes where you could perhaps find the date?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I would carry out a literary search and find the dates of what is known in the media as the "first marketplace attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where do you have those notes? Do you have them with you in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I would have to go and look on my computer, which is in my room in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us assume that you will be able to come back to the issue tomorrow if you think you can find the date. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am certain I will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if it assists Your Honours, and for the anticipated objection, if he has left Sarajevo at that time, if he was not present during the time the incident happened, I am not sure whether it assists even to find the date and to take it further. I am just not sure how much he can be cross-examined on something he had no recollection of, other than from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I would like to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...first respond briefly. It was not the answer of this witness that he had only from the media. I think he told us that he saw a report given to him, or at least provided to him so that he could read it. So it is not just the media, Mr. Waespi, and of course one of the puzzling things might be is whether it is a specific date all too well known to many of us so that we can identify more in detail whether we are talking about something which is relatively new or which is relatively well known - perhaps not well enough - but at least is well known to us. And then of course we would have to see what the testimony could add to and on what basis. So, therefore, I think it is too early to decide on such an objection, but since you made it already at this stage, I think the Chamber should give it the view that we cannot yet -- we cannot yet confirm to you that it could not assist the Chamber. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I will go -- come back to this issue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, and since you have to come back anyway, I would like you to check on the date. I would like to come back to what we have examined at the end of our preceding session. You told us, Witness, that on numerous occasions, the B forces fired from the inside of a hospital called the Kosevo hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, to the best of your knowledge, were there any other similar situations involving other hospitals where the same pattern was reproduced?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: The only one that I am aware of is at Kosevo hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us on a number of occasions what you meant by that -- by that, did you say, once, twice, three times or a dozen times?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I know of two times and I believe, from things which were told to me by other UN personnel, that it happened probably five, six times, but that is not something I can confirm hard and fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. You spoke to us about a mobile mortar mounted on the back of a truck. Now, it was not on the truck, perhaps, it was behind it. The testimony was that it was -- that the principle that it was put on the back of a lorry or a truck, that is right. Was it -- was it an 82-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the calibre of the mortar because I did not personally see the truck with the mortars on it. The journalists who witnessed the firing on the 24th of December, 1992 and the sergeant who delivered the diesel fuel to Kosevo hospital, both saw what I believe was the same type of vehicle, and described it, but they were not artillery people who were able to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us where was the point of departure of the shot that hit General Morillon's residence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was somewhere near the Presidency building in Sarajevo. I would have to look at my notes and the reports which I wrote at the time in order to be able to tell you more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you could do it at the same time you will check up on the date. Since a report was written, the people who manned the mortar, were they militarily trained in the sense of uniforms that they might have worn?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That I cannot answer, as I did not personally see them. It was these other people who saw them. What I do believe is that they were part of a special unit of the kind that you described earlier which was based somewhere to the south-west of Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke in your testimony of a unit, mortars unit or specialised in mortars, a unit specialised in mortars. Witness, do you know whether there were several specialised units in the area of mortars? And here I have in mind greater Sarajevo, that is, the 10 municipalities composing Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I only have information around one particular mobile special mortar unit which was under the control of a radical part of the BiH army. I do not have any information whether there were other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When you spoke -- speak about this, you have to be very precise. We are talking about mobile special mortar units. We are referring to the unit as being mobile. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that the units had these trucks and was able to move somewhere, fire quickly, and then move away quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. You told us that in the case that you suspected, there was a shot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provoked by the BH forces just before a press conference was held. Can you perhaps be more specific in terms of date and period of time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Again, I would have to look back through my notes. It was not something which was particularly important to me at that time. It is something that I know happened, but I would have to think back hard to try and work out what the date would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. This was the third note, mental note, you have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the witness can be provided with a slip of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you go through the three items? The first one is the date of the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, we have the date of the first incident. Now we are referring to the date of the shot on the Kosevo area. And the second I would like to ask for the assistance of the Chambers because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I could help you. You asked the witness to look back at a certain -- yes, on the headquarters of General Morillon. But I didn't want to interrupt you, but I think we do have, as a matter of fact, a document which will be tendered under seal, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have it, well and fine. Very good. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...well, that became the second now is the date of the press conference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now in respect of the date, the date we do not know for the time being, you spoke about a deliberate shot, but what was the reason for it? What was the aim, the objective?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot say what the objective of the people carrying it out was, although it seemed to me that it was in order to deliberately provoke the shelling of the hospital in order to -- in such a way that the international media would see this event before their eyes and maybe even suffer some of the shelling themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, if I understood you well, that there was a will to provoke reaction at a given point in time with the purpose of manipulating public opinion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Whether it was to manipulate public opinion, I cannot say. What I can say is that there were quite a number of actions, by that I mean shooting or attacks, carried out in order to break ceasefires and provoke reactions which would perpetuate the collapse of the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say that these actions were aimed at perpetuating the collapse of the ceasefire, do you mean by that that the actions were carried out by a particular side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it the BH side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you consider that, since you have used the term "to perpetuate," that this was part of a plan, that is, of a political will?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Whether it was of political will, again, I cannot say. What I can say is that it was our - and by "our" I mean General Morillon and my own and general headquarters - belief that from about December 1992 onwards, the Bosnian Serb side wanted peace. They wanted an overall ceasefire in order to consolidate the territory of which they had taken control of. In that aim, to that aim, the Bosnian Serb side was trying to achieve ceasefires. From the Bosniak side, however, they did not want to submit to a situation which had been enforced upon them and, therefore, they did not want to recognise the status quo, and accepting a ceasefire would have meant accepting the status quo. Now, they could not publicly state that, but their activities on the ground were uniformly aimed at preventing any kind of permanent ceasefire across all of Bosnia-Herzegovina from taking hold in order to perpetuate the fighting, in order to give them the opportunity eventually in order to retake some of the terrain which had been taken control of by the Bosnian Serbs in the period from April 1992 up until December 1992. I was at a meeting with General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic in November 1992, at which they got out a map which showed the ethnic distribution of Bosnia, in colour, and they used this map in order to illustrate to General Morillon how they had only taken control of areas where the Serb population was in 50 per cent majority or greater and that they had not tried to take control over areas where the Serb population was in the minority. And that they had done this in a way which was fair, in the way that they described it, and that the results of this was that the front line was not a front line which was militarily sensible. In other words, the front line was very long; it waved all over the place, and from a tactical or strategic military point of view, it made no sense whatsoever. However, that was the reason why they had chosen to -- over the period of April 1992 to December 1992 taken the military actions that they had, and it is in that context that I made the point earlier that the attack on Sarajevo at the end of October was the last major Bosnian Serb military activity, military offensive. From then on, they basically carried out defensive operations and tried to terrorise the Bosniak population and the Presidency into accepting this status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I would like to re-read the last element of your reply. Yes. Witness, you have the screen before your eyes. In lines 14 and 15, you expressed by using an indefinite pronoun. You say -- when you say and speak about this, "they," whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not familiar with the -- I can't identify line 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. So don't say a single word. Stop here, please. Line 14 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I have a whole series of numbers on the left-hand side and it is not clear to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: 14, the first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 14 is not the first line any more. Yes the pages and lines are in the gray area to the left. But I think it has disappeared already. If you could please read --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "That was the reason why they are chosen the period of April 1992 to December 1992 -- " and it is out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not line 14. That might be the problem, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I will read it. Your testimony was that: "In order to perpetuate the fighting, in order to give them the opportunity eventually, in order to retake some of the terrain which had been taken control of by the Bosnian Serbs in the period from April 1992 up until December 1992. I was at a meeting with General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry, I have to interrupt you. I apologise, but it is line 14 of the page 48. I am sorry. What the witness said was the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...so I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because that was the problem with my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...couple of pages. So then please just read it. And that created to the confusion, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What I have before my eyes, however, [In English] "Why they had chosen the period of April 1992 to December 1992," [Interpretation] et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Who do you mean by saying, "they"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I mean that Bosnian Serb leadership, in other words, Dr. Karadzic, et cetera, had during the period April 1992 to December 1992 taken control of a portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the explanation for taking those parts was what they were explaining to General Morillon with this map. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Sir, now in relation to what you said, and I apologise because my computer doesn't have the exactly -- my transcript doesn't have exactly the same numbering, but in relation to what you said, could we consider that in the period that you are talking about, that is the period when there were ceasefire negotiations, on the Serb side in Sarajevo, there was a military and political will not to continue attacking the city, not to be the aggressor on the city. For the English booth, not "not to continue," but not to egress, in order to obtain a ceasefire. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It is partially true. It was the results of our own headquarters analysis that from about December 1992 onwards, the Bosnian Serb side wanted a global ceasefire. What they did not want was local ceasefires. What the Bosniak side wanted was local ceasefires. But to come back to Sarajevo, yes, I believe that there were probably no major attempts to capture Sarajevo, as I described, but there was nonstop shelling of the citizens of Sarajevo, and the siege of Sarajevo and the prevention of food aid and the repair of utilities continued throughout. And that we interpreted as being a continuation of the terrorism of the population of Sarajevo in order to make them accept the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, sir. I would like to, after your lengthy answer, to go back to the elements of mobile mortars. These elements, it is true that you yourself never saw them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you, sir, however, see even smaller elements that would correspond to private personal vehicles, of a passenger vehicle like Golf, for instance, where there would be mortars mounted on top of them? They would have been placed inside vehicles and with which small units could move around that shoot for a while and then move, then withdraw. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I know that that happened. I did not see it myself, but I read reports from our intelligence people who had had reports from soldiers on the ground who had seen such vehicles and such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you said that you had two kinds of information. One was the intelligence, intelligence information, and the other kind would have been from soldiers on the ground themselves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, are we here talking about multiple elements, that is, of a number of these vehicles that would have been used for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: It was our impression that the Bosniaks were using any kind of vehicle that they had inside Sarajevo for military purposes. It was only for those vehicles that they made fuel available because there was a shortage, a very strict shortage of fuel in Sarajevo, and the Armija largely controlled, together with the black market, the availability of fuel for cars in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification on a question you just put to the witness. The witness testified that he did not see by himself the cars with mortars in it but that he read reports from his intelligence people who had had reports from soldiers on the ground who had seen such vehicles and such people. Your next question was: Sir, you said that you had two kinds of information, where it seems from your answer that you had as a source of information the reports of your intelligence people relating what they heard from soldiers on the ground. So the next question to you is, you said you had two kinds of information: One was the intelligence information and the other kind would have been from soldiers on the ground. But your source of information, was that soldiers on the ground reporting to intelligence and then intelligence reports read by you; or did you have this information from two different sources, that means from the intelligence and from soldiers on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had from both sources. So your first answer was a bit confusing then for me, that it came only through the intelligence reports. It clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now that we have these two sources of information clear as they are and because you said that the army was using practically all the vehicles that they had at their disposal, do you include in your answer then also the vehicles that we would call "civilian vehicles"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say "civilian vehicles," were these sometimes, occasionally, or all the time, vehicles that were not even marked as being used for military purposes, being military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, there was a situation in Sarajevo whereby, as we hear it from you, sir, is that most of the civilian vehicles were used by the military for military purposes and at the same time when not officially distinguished or marked as such as military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Some vehicles, some civilian vehicles were painted and marked as Armija, but there were others which were not. The situation in Sarajevo was that the Bosniak Presidency forces had virtually no, what I would call proper military vehicles, and that they made use of the only equipment which was available to them, which was predominantly civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if, in practice, there was a situation of a requisition, de facto requisition?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I do not know how people came to be in possession of vehicles. What I can say is that most vehicles driving around Sarajevo with the shortage of fuel were being used, to the best of my knowledge, for military purposes of one kind or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to the civilian vehicles that were used for transporting mortars. And I have to say that we have had testimonies saying that they were basically, most of the time, Golf cars, so Volkswagen Golf vehicles. Do you know, perhaps of other vehicles, private vehicles, passenger vehicles, that were used by these mobile mortar units?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot say specifically Volkswagen Golf. I must be clear, I am talking about two separate activities. One is what I called a mobile mortar unit, and that is the one where the description given to me was of small trucks, something like -- this is my imagination now, putting into words what I was told, something like a Land Rover or a pick-up, yes. Now, a second piece of information is reports picked up by soldiers on the ground reported to the intelligence reports which came to me, and secondly, from my own speaking with the Danish company which shuttled back and forth between General Morillon's headquarters in Sarajevo and the headquarters in Kiseljak, and they were always driving back and forth through Sarajevo. And I spoke with those soldiers every day in order to get a sense of what was happening, what the atmosphere was like. And it is -- those were the soldiers on the ground who I personally spoke with and they told me that they had seen the sort of thing you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But were you told of specific vehicles, for instance, that was a Golf or that was a Bentley for instance, just to give you an example which would not be very ordinary?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: However, now starting from the facts that these vehicles existed, could we then assume that they were quite difficult to locate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean by "quite difficult to locate."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to rephrase my question, in fact. If these vehicles were very mobile, is it then true to say that on one hand they could move around everywhere, and on the other hand, they would then be discreet in their shooting, in their firing, that is, they would fire a few shots and then they would disappear. They would go somewhere else. It would be hard to trace where it came from. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, but that is correct. But I must also put this in context, which is that the vast majority of vehicles used for what I described as military purposes was simply to transport personnel around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I don't doubt that. We will come back to that. Sir, I was talking about vehicles that were carrying mortars. So could you perhaps give us your answer again, is that true?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, such vehicles could have driven anywhere within Sarajevo that the Bosniak authorities allowed them to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any reason why the Bosnian authorities would have banned them from going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of different factions in Sarajevo and there were sometimes crackdowns by what I would describe as the "authorised" police against what I would describe as hardline extremists, and sometimes the hardline extremists would try and stop and prevent the movement of what I would call "mainline people." And this varied from time to time, depending on the politics and the power plays that were going on in the Presidency at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We will probably come back to it later. I think that you may have been referring to a name. Are you familiar with the name of Juka or the first name Juka?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. We are talking about the same person so we will speak about it at a later stage. Now, you said that vehicles were used to transport military personnel; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But when we are talking about civilian vehicles, these are mostly vehicles of a family car, a passenger car, for instance, a passenger vehicle which could, perhaps, carry four or five, maybe even six people. Are we talking about this type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, such a vehicle, would you then consider it as a military target, if this vehicle is transporting military personnel?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I would consider it, as a military officer, to be a military target, but I would also have to take into account the risk of my being wrong and it not being a military target before I personally decided to shoot at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am trying to listen carefully. I did not want to interrupt you during your questioning, but especially the beginning of page 73, the answer of the witness in relation to your questions were somewhat confusing. So I would like to ask some clarification. Is it your testimony that most of the vehicles within the city, civilian vehicles, were, at the disposition of the military, they would be used so or was there a certain percentage of the civilian vehicles that was used or was at a disposition of the military? It was not quite clear to me what your testimony was in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not asked for a percentage and would not be able to give one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may I just read one line to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I perhaps continue with another line of questioning and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to then ask the witness the following. You -- one of the questions to you was: "Therefore, there was a situation in Sarajevo whereby, as we hear it from you sir, is that most of the civilian vehicles were used by the military for military purposes?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So most of the civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said that in your capacity as an artillery officer, you would then consider this as a military target, but that you would then make sure, you would take care in some way, you would think twice in order to find out if there was a risk of making an error. That was the meaning of what you said?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just one point. I am not sure whether he said in his capacity as an artillery officer that he answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a witness, and this witness is an artillery officer. So I don't know whether this is of major importance. Let's say "as an officer." Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly the terms of what the witness said as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As an officer is fine. I am just saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: He has said "as an officer." [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So I just said artillery officer, because you are an artillery officer. So that was exactly what you said in your testimony, that is how you put it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: I am an artillery officer, but being in the artillery is irrelevant to my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you. But my question is the following: If you are an officer, not "you," but if one is an officer, and that one knows, as you just said yourself, that in practice all distribution of fuel is controlled by the army, BH army, isn't it then true to say that, logically speaking, it would be fair to say that such vehicles were therefore at the disposal of the army? They were placed at the disposal of the army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is not completely the case. I said that fuel was controlled by the army or by the black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, there are two possibilities here: Either the army or the criminals who are involved in the black market?

utterances.speaker: PYERS WILLIAM TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At when are we finishing? At quarter to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will soon adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. May I ask you not to speak with anyone about your testimony until tomorrow, until we resume. That is also valid for the -- those who are working in the Office of the Prosecution. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to inform the parties that this morning it was mentioned that there would be a Plenary which would take three days. As far as I am informed at this moment, the Plenary is trying to reduce the time necessary for its discussions. That would mean that almost for certain on that Wednesday, which is I think the 14th - but I am not quite sure about that - that we would have an ordinary hearing, and even perhaps, but we still have to consider that, on Friday afternoon. That would mean that we would lose only one day instead of three days during the Plenary. I am just informing you. This is not a final announcement, but in order to make sure that you are not too much surprised at a later stage. Then the last thing I would like to -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, according to my calculations, there is approximately one hour left for cross-examination. Yes. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
